id: A Note Left in Jimmy Leonard’s Shack

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Near the dry river’s water-mark we found Your brother Minnegan, Flopped like a fish against the muddy ground. Beany, the kid whose yellow hair turns green, Told me to find you, even in the rain, And tell you he was drowned. I hid behind the chassis on the bank, The wreck of someone’s Ford: I was afraid to come and wake you drunk: You told me once the waking up was hard, The daylight beating at you like a board. Blood in my stomach sank. Beside, you told him never to go out Along the river-side Drinking and singing, clattering about. You might have thrown a rock at me and cried I was to blame, I let him fall in the road And pitch down on his side. Well, I’ll get hell enough when I get home For coming up this far, Leaving the note, and running as I came. I’ll go and tell my father where you are. You’d better go find Minnegan before Policemen hear and come. Beany went home, and I got sick and ran, You old son of a bitch. You better hurry down to Minnegan; He’s drunk or dying now, I don’t know which, Rolled in the roots and garbage like a fish, The poor old man.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker reports finding Minnegan near the dry river’s water-mark, lying in the mud as if drowned or gravely injured.
- Beany sends the speaker to inform Minnegan’s brother despite the rain and the danger of waking him while drunk.
- The speaker is frightened of being blamed for Minnegan’s condition because Minnegan had been warned not to go drinking by the river.
- The speaker plans to leave a note, tell their father where the brother is, and return home despite expecting punishment.
- The speaker urgently tells Minnegan’s brother to find him before the police arrive, uncertain whether Minnegan is drunk or dying.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A frightened speaker reports Minnegan’s apparent drowning or collapse by the dry river, using a frantic first-person message to warn his brother while revealing fear, guilt, and family violence. The key result is that Minnegan is left “drunk or dying” among mud and garbage, making the poem a stark portrait of neglect, poverty, and the urgent human cost of addiction.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Near, Your, Minnegan

outputs.L1:
Near the dry river’s watermark, we found your brother, Minnegan,  
flopped like a fish upon the muddy ground.  
Beany—the kid whose yellow hair turns green—  
told me to find you, even in the rain,  
and tell you he had drowned.

I hid behind the chassis on the bank,  
the wreck of someone’s Ford.  
I was afraid to come and wake you drunk;  
you told me once that waking up was hard,  
the daylight striking you like a board.  
The blood sank in my stomach.

Besides, you told him never to go out  
along the riverside,  
drinking and singing, clattering about.  
You might have thrown a rock at me and cried  
that I was to blame—  
that I had let him fall in the road  
and pitch down on his side.

Well, I’ll catch hell enough when I get home  
for coming up this far,  
leaving the note, and running as I came.  
I’ll go and tell my father where you are.  
You had better go find Minnegan before  
the policemen hear and come.

Beany went home, and I got sick and ran,  
you old son of a bitch.  
You had better hurry down to Minnegan;  
he is drunk or dying now—I do not know which—  
rolled among the roots and garbage like a fish,  
the poor old man.
outputs.L2:
By the dried-up riverbed, close to where the water once reached, we found your brother Minnegan. He was sprawled in the mud, floundered there like a fish thrown onto land.

Beany—the boy with the yellow hair that looks green—sent me to look for you, even though it was raining, and to tell you that Minnegan had drowned.

I stayed hidden behind an old car frame on the bank, the ruined body of somebody’s Ford. I was scared to come wake you while you were drunk. You told me once that being woken was terrible, that daylight hit you like a plank.

I felt my insides drop.

And besides, you had warned him not to go wandering down by the river, drinking, singing, and making all that noise. You might have hurled a stone at me and shouted that it was my fault—that I had let him stumble from the road and fall over on his side.

Anyway, I’ll be in enough trouble when I get back home for having come all the way here, leaving the message, and then running off the way I did. I’m going to tell my father where to find you.

You should go down and look for Minnegan before the police hear about it and arrive. Beany went back home, and I got nauseous and ran, you miserable old bastard.

You’d better get to Minnegan quickly. He may only be drunk, or he may be dying—I can’t tell. He’s lying tangled in roots and trash like a fish, the poor old man.
outputs.L3:
The speaker explains that Minnegan has been found near the water-mark of the dry river, lying in the mud in a terrible state. At first, it is unclear whether he has drowned, been badly hurt, or simply collapsed there after drinking. His condition is frightening enough that Beany decides someone must go at once to tell Minnegan’s brother.

Even though it is raining and the situation is dangerous, Beany sends the speaker to deliver the message. The speaker is especially afraid because Minnegan’s brother may be drunk and difficult to wake. There is also the risk that he will be angry or violent when disturbed. Still, Beany insists that the brother must be told, because Minnegan may need help immediately.

The speaker is terrified that people might blame them for what has happened. Minnegan had already been warned not to go drinking by the river, and now he has been found there in the mud. Because of this, the speaker fears that others may think they were involved, or that they failed to stop him. The uncertainty of Minnegan’s condition makes the fear even worse: no one knows whether he is merely drunk, seriously injured, or close to death.

The speaker decides on a plan. They will leave a note, tell their father where Minnegan’s brother can be found, and then return home. Even though they expect to be punished for being out or for becoming involved in the matter, they feel they have no choice. The most important thing is to get help for Minnegan before it is too late.

When the speaker reaches Minnegan’s brother, they urgently tell him to go and find Minnegan before the police arrive. The speaker cannot say for certain what has happened; Minnegan may only be drunk, but he may also be dying. Because of that uncertainty, the message is desperate and immediate: Minnegan’s brother must act quickly, before the situation becomes worse and before the authorities take control.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a frightened first-person speaker urgently reporting that Minnegan has collapsed, or perhaps drowned, near the dry river. The speaker’s voice is frantic and unstable, as if he is trying to deliver a warning before it is too late. By addressing his brother directly, he turns the poem into a desperate message, one filled with panic, confusion, and emotional pressure. The speaker does not fully understand what has happened, but he knows that Minnegan is in terrible danger. His repeated uncertainty—whether Minnegan is “drunk or dying”—makes the scene even more disturbing, because it suggests that suffering and addiction have become so common that death can almost be mistaken for another episode of drunkenness.

The setting reinforces this sense of abandonment. Minnegan is found not in a safe or caring place, but among mud, trash, and the dry riverbed. The river, usually associated with life, movement, and cleansing, is dry, which makes the landscape feel empty and hopeless. The garbage and mud surrounding Minnegan suggest poverty and neglect, as though both the man and the place have been forgotten. This physical environment mirrors the emotional condition of the family: damaged, violent, and unable to protect its own members.

The speaker’s fear is mixed with guilt. He seems horrified by what he has seen, but he also appears implicated in the family’s pain. The mention of family violence suggests that Minnegan’s collapse is not an isolated event. It is part of a larger pattern of harm, addiction, and desperation. The speaker’s warning to his brother reveals a family in crisis, where people hurt one another but are also terrified of losing one another. This tension gives the poem its emotional force: the speaker is both a witness to suffering and a participant in a damaged family history.

Ultimately, the poem becomes a stark portrait of human neglect. Minnegan’s body lying in the mud and garbage shows the brutal cost of addiction, poverty, and violence. The phrase “drunk or dying” captures the tragic uncertainty at the center of the poem: Minnegan is still alive enough to be seen, but he has already been socially and emotionally abandoned. The poem forces the reader to confront the urgency of his condition and the larger world that has allowed him to end up there. It is not only a report of one man’s collapse, but also a powerful image of a family and community failing under the weight of fear, guilt, and suffering.
outputs.L5:
**Near Your Minnegan**

Near your Minnegan, the world feels a little quieter and more familiar. It is the kind of place where memories seem to gather softly, where every path, corner, and breeze carries a sense of belonging. Whether Minnegan is a town, a home, or a special place in someone’s heart, being near it brings comfort and connection.

There is something meaningful about staying close to the places that shape us. Near your Minnegan, you may find old stories, friendly faces, and reminders of where you have been. It can be a place of peace, inspiration, and reflection—a place that helps you feel grounded even when life becomes uncertain.

In the end, Minnegan is more than just a name. It represents closeness, memory, and the feeling of being connected to something important. Being near your Minnegan means being near a part of yourself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark narrative poem in a rough, vernacular voice about a frightened boy telling someone that their brother Minnegan has been found drowned near a dry river, with details like Beany, a wrecked Ford, rain, drunkenness, and police coming.
counterfactuals.output:
Mister—  
don’t hit me for comin’ so late,  
I run all the way from Beany’s place,  
past the wrecked Ford with its nose in the ditch  
and the weeds all black with rain.

I’m soaked through, see?  
Ain’t mud, that on my pants.  
Ain’t only mud.

It’s Minnegan.

They found your brother Minnegan  
down by the river that ain’t been a river  
since God got tired of us—  
dry bed, cracked clay, bottles, bones,  
old tires sittin’ like dead dogs in the dust.

Only tonight it rained mean,  
come down hard as gravel,  
filled up the low places,  
made a brown mouth outta nothin’.  
And Minnegan, drunk as Sunday sorrow,  
went wanderin’ there after Beany laughed  
and said he couldn’t even walk a straight fence.

He near proved him right.

The Ford’s smashed up, mister,  
one wheel still turnin’ when we come on it,  
headlights shinin’ sideways at the sky  
like it was askin’ mercy.  
Beany said Minnegan was singin’  
when he climbed out—  
singin’ and cursin’ the rain,  
with blood under his hair  
and whiskey on his coat.

Then he slipped off.

Nobody knowed where till morning,  
when the water had gone thin again  
and left him in a pocket of clay,  
face down, hands open,  
like he was beggin’ the dirt  
to take back whatever it give him.

I seen him, mister.  
I wish I hadn’t.

His hat was caught on a root.  
His mouth was full of river  
where there weren’t no river.  
His boots was pointed toward home  
like he’d changed his mind too late.

Beany’s cryin’ now,  
but he’s drunk cryin’,  
the kind that don’t wash nothin’ clean.  
Says it weren’t his fault.  
Says Minnegan laughed.  
Says the Ford jumped the road  
like a spooked horse.

Police are comin’.  
I heard the siren down the county line,  
thin and blue and angry.  
They’ll ask who drove.  
They’ll ask who drank.  
They’ll ask why no one went lookin’  
when the rain was still poundin’  
and a man could drown  
in a place too dry to pray over.

Mister—  
don’t make me say it again.

Your brother Minnegan’s dead.  
The river took him  
without ever comin’ back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of mid-20th-century American narrative verse, spoken by a scared child, reporting that an old drunk named Minnegan is lying by the riverbank, possibly dead.
counterfactuals.output:
Ma, come quick—  
don’t send me back there alone.

Down by the river,  
past the busted fence  
where the cows won’t cross,  
old Minnegan is lying  
with his coat in the mud  
and one boot in the water.

I called him, Ma.  
I did.  
I said, “Mister Minnegan,”  
like you told me to say  
to grown men,  
even the bad ones,  
even the ones who smell  
like stove smoke and bottles.

But he didn’t cuss me  
or wave his hand.  
He didn’t even spit.

The river was talking hard  
over the stones,  
and the weeds kept bending  
like they knew something.  
His hat was upside down  
beside him,  
full of rain.

I saw his face, Ma—  
only a little.  
White as flour  
where the mud wasn’t on it.  
There was a fly  
walking near his eye.

Don’t make me tell Pa first.  
Pa will say I’m lying  
or else he’ll run,  
and I can’t run again.  
My legs are shaking now.

Maybe he’s sleeping.  
Maybe drunk men sleep that way,  
half in the world  
and half in the cold river.

But, Ma—  
when I threw a stone  
near his hand,  
not at him,  
just near—  
he never moved.

Come quick.  
Bring the lantern.  
Bring somebody tall.  
And hold my sleeve  
when we go down there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bleak dramatic monologue where the speaker is afraid to wake a drunk man and tells him his brother Minnegan has been found near the river, “flopped like a fish” in mud and garbage.
counterfactuals.output:
Don’t make me touch your shoulder.

Don’t make me be the one to drag you up out of that bottle-dark sleep, with your mouth open and your coat still on, one boot under the table like it tried to leave without you. I’ve stood here ten minutes listening to you breathe. Ten minutes is a long time when a man is lying somewhere else not breathing at all.

Wake up.

No—don’t. God help me, don’t wake yet.

Because once you open your eyes, I’ll have to say it plain, and the words will become a thing in the room with us. They’ll sit down in the chair between the stove and the door. They’ll take off their hat. They’ll wait for you to understand.

It’s Minnegan.

Your brother Minnegan has been found near the river, “flopped like a fish” in mud and garbage, down where the black water chews at the pilings and the gulls scream like women. That’s how they said it. Not me. I wouldn’t have chosen those words. I would’ve wrapped him in something kinder, if there’s anything kind left to wrap a man in.

They found him among the cans and rotten paper, one arm twisted under him, face turned toward the river as if he’d been trying to drink the whole damned thing dry. His hair was full of silt. His pockets were out. His shoes—Christ, his shoes were gone.

And now here you are, drunk as judgment, sleeping through the last minutes of being a man who doesn’t know.

I’m afraid of you when you wake. Not your fists. Not your shouting. I’m afraid of that little silence that comes after the news goes in. The silence where something inside a person walks away and doesn’t come back.

So sleep, if you can.

Sleep one minute more in this filthy peace, with the bottle for a pillow and the rain scratching at the window. Sleep before I say your name hard enough to break the night open.

Because when you wake, the river comes with me.

And Minnegan too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty free-verse poem with characters named Minnegan and Beany, involving a drowned man by a river, a boy hiding behind a wrecked Ford, and a threatening, alcoholic family atmosphere.
counterfactuals.output:
Minnegan kept a bottle  
under the sink  
where the pipes sweated brown  
and the roaches learned the family prayers.

Beany knew the sound of it—  
glass neck kissing tooth,  
the long swallow,  
the chair-leg scrape  
like a knife being pulled from a boot.

Outside, the river dragged itself past town,  
green-black and swollen,  
carrying branches, oil-slick foam,  
one dead dog once,  
and now a man.

Face down in the reeds  
with his coat ballooned full of water,  
he knocked softly against the mud  
as if asking in,  
as if any door around there  
opened for mercy.

Minnegan spat and said  
don’t look,  
which meant look,  
which meant remember  
what happens to men  
who owe or drink or talk too much.

Beany was twelve  
and already had the posture  
of someone apologizing to walls.

He ran when the shouting started,  
when Ma’s voice cracked  
and Minnegan’s belt came loose  
with that dry leather whisper.

He hid behind the wrecked Ford  
in the yard,  
the one with no tires,  
its windshield starred like a frozen pond,  
its seats split open  
and leaking yellow foam  
like old bones.

From there he could see the river  
and the drowned man  
turning slowly,  
one pale hand lifting now and then  
in the current.

From there he could hear the house—  
Minnegan roaring,  
a plate breaking,  
Ma saying please  
in the thin voice she hated,  
the baby coughing in the back room,  
the bottle tipping again  
like weather,  
like law.

The whole place leaned drunk:  
the porch,  
the fence,  
the sky nailed low  
over the weeds.

Beany pressed his cheek  
to the Ford’s cold rust  
and tasted blood  
where he’d bitten through his lip.

He wondered if the drowned man  
had a name  
someone called softly once.

He wondered if the river  
was kinder than a kitchen  
after midnight.

Minnegan came outside then,  
boots sinking in the mud,  
shirt half open,  
eyes bright and mean  
as broken glass.

“Beany,” he called,  
sweet as poison.  
“Boy.”

The river kept moving.

The dead man kept knocking.

And Beany, behind the wrecked Ford,  
made himself smaller  
than breath,  
smaller than prayer,  
smaller than the last clean thing  
left in that yard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a tragic poem narrated in colloquial language about a child delivering bad news: Minnegan has fallen by the riverside after drinking, Beany sent the speaker, and the police may arrive soon.
counterfactuals.output:
I come runnin’, ma’am—don’t ask me to sit,  
my shoes are full of river mud  
and my chest is kickin’ like a busted drum.

Beany sent me.  
He said, “Go tell ’em quick,  
tell ’em Minnegan’s down by the riverside,  
tell ’em he’d been drinkin’ again,  
tell ’em he didn’t get back up.”

I seen him there—  
not like folks sleep,  
not peaceful, not tucked in right,  
just crooked in the reeds  
with the brown water talkin’ low beside him.

His cap was off.  
One hand was open  
like he’d dropped somethin’  
nobody could pick up.

Beany stayed with him,  
kept sayin’, “Lord, Minnie,  
why’d you go and do it?”  
though Minnegan couldn’t hear,  
or wouldn’t answer,  
or was already past all that.

And listen—  
you best come now if you’re comin’,  
’cause somebody went for the police,  
and they’ll be down there soon  
with their hard boots  
and their questions  
and their faces like doors shut tight.

I’m just a kid, ma’am.  
I don’t know how to say it pretty.  
Minnegan fell by the riverside  
after the drink got hold of him,  
and Beany sent me runnin’  
so the news wouldn’t arrive alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
